newsitem.title: UK: Top UK soldier joins calls for total nuclear ban.
newsitem.headline: Top UK soldier joins calls for total nuclear ban.

text.p: A retired field marshal, once the most senior military officer in Britain, on Thursday joined international calls for the elimination of all nuclear weapons.

"We have a golden opportunity at the moment, as the relations between the major powers are quite good, and that is the time surely to persuade them to make this radical move," Field-Marshal Lord Michael Carver said.

Carver's announcement followed a statement issued on Wednesday by General Lee Butler, former commander-in-chief of the U.S. Strategic Forces and the man who would have given the order for the launch of nuclear weapons during the Cold War.

The statement, signed by at least 60 retired senior officers from around the world, said: "Long-term international nuclear policy must be based on the declared principle of continuous, complete and irrevocable elimination of nuclear weapons."
Carver, 81 and formerly Chief of the Defence Staff, said the reduction of the international nuclear arsenal inevitably had to be driven by the United States and Russia.
"If they don't (begin reduction) it will never happen," he said, adding other nuclear powers would need an assurance they were not acting in isolation.

Those who have signed the statement all previously held top military posts in their countries. They include General Alexander Lebed, former national security adviser for Russia's President Boris Yeltsin.

Carver stressed the comparative risks of disarmament, if efficiently monitored, were significantly lower than the risk of accidents, proliferation and irresponsible use of nuclear power if the current situation were allowed to continue.

He recalled the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the only two times nuclear weapons have been used in war, and emphasised that those bombs were of quite a low yield and much simpler than many of the weapons existing now.
"The result of a nuclear exchange could well mean the destruction of the whole of the northern hemisphere," he said.

The main opposition to the call for total abolition was the United States nuclear and defence establishment, who had a very strong political lobby and would be very difficult to overcome, Carver said.

"The key to our success would be to persuade the president of the United States that disarmament would be in their best security interests," Carver concluded. Carver was chief of the defence staff from 1973 to 1976 when he retired.
